utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Tubakovic, please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we start, since we are starting now, we shall shift our break to 1100 hours. Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tubakovic.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tubakovic, could you please tell me if you can hear me properly and if you're also receiving the translation.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you, and the translation is good.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tubakovic, for the purposes of the transcript, could you please tell us your full first and last name.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I am Marko Tubakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Mr. Tubakovic, as the Defence counsel for Mr. Zaric, we are just going to introduce you to the Trial Chamber, and after that, the other Defence counsels and the Prosecution will cross-examine you. You have already testified under Rule 71. You have given your deposition in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, you described certain episodes relating to Mr. Zaric and also regarding certain -- a certain document which we have called an information here, and that is document P127. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So now I will let my colleagues cross-examine you. As far as the warnings you have received about answering questions, you remember that, don't you? So please, could you wait until the question is completed, wait for a couple of seconds after you receive the translation in your headphones, and then start to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We will not examine the witness in chief. We already had the answers that we wanted from this witness during depositions in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. So the Prosecution. Because our decision was that the Prosecution would start.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I clarify that? My understanding of the ruling, I've been searching through the transcript was we put on a motion, the relief sought was that the Trial Chamber call proprio motu the witness. The relief was quite specific in the order, in the motion, sought that then the Defence of Mr. Zaric be given a chance if they wished to elicit further examination-in-chief, then the Defence and the Prosecution cross-examine. I can't find it in the transcript the specific ruling. Your Honour's ruling I thought was we grant the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. Yes. The Defence can start.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe I can give the answer to Mr. Re. Mr. Tubakovic was proposed as a witness on some particular events, and we already have all the answers through Mr. Tubakovic. We have not any intention to examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That is understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- Mr. Tubakovic. We understand the position of the Prosecution, so we just waive right to examine him in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on behalf of Mr. Tadic's Defence, we will not cross-examine this witness unless there is something that arises from the questions from the Prosecution. But in view of what he stated during his testimony in chief, while giving his deposition, we do not have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Tubakovic. I am Mr. Pantelic, the counsel for Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tubakovic, you responded to questions from my colleague Mr. Pisarevic in Belgrade during the procedure when the depositions were given, and you spoke about the information compiled by the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade. You also talked about a meeting between representatives of the civilian authorities of the Samac municipality and members of the command.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please, could you tell us, if you remember, it's been a long time ago, but do you remember when this meeting was held, in view of the fact that the information has the date the 12th of January, 1992 [as interpreted], could you please tell us when this meeting took place.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: This meeting took place three days after --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... here in the transcript that the date is 12th of January, 1992. This couldn't be a correct date, definitely so. Maybe my colleague could pose the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I said the 1st of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The information was adopted in late November, around the 1st of December, and the meeting of the inner circle of the command and the structures of the political powers of Samac and Pelagicevo under formation was held two or three days after it was adopted. I don't know the exact date, but I think it was probably held by December 5th, at the latest. It happened very quickly after the information was adopted, in early December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also during your testimony you mentioned the persons who were present at that meeting. What I would like to ask you now, and in view of your previous statement and the fact that you mentioned that Mr. Blagoje Simic was also among those present, could you please explain to the Trial Chamber: What was Dr. Simic's position at that meeting? I know that you perhaps cannot recall all the details and everything that was discussed then, but as far as you can recall, can you please tell the Trial Chamber: How did Mr. Simic behave at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: The majority of the criticism by the command for the formulation of this information and the way it was formulated came from the chief of the public security station, Stevan Todorovic, who was also present at that meeting, and the president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Samac, Milan Simic. As far as I can recall right now, because it did happen a long time ago, Dr. Blagoje, at the end, appealed for the unity of the command of the Tactical Group and of the 2nd Posavina Brigade and the political authorities. That is as much as I can remember, because while receiving information about this document, the information, there were different opinions expressed and different positions taken about the events by the command and by the political structures. He tried to say - I can't remember all the details - but he insisted on achieving some kind of unity and of continuing in the implementation of certain activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, if you remember, of course, whether he addressed those present from the positions of power and from the position of his post, or whether he just did that as a person giving his political assessment.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, Dr. Simic was the president of the War Presidency of the Assembly, or whatever it was called. But he addressed those present in the way I described before. He didn't issue any kind of ultimatum, nor did he come out very strongly towards the members of the command in relation to the statements by some other people who were present at that meeting, because, if I remember rightly, I know that there were some statements made by some people that the command didn't know what it was doing, and so on and so forth. As far as I can remember, Dr. Simic definitely did not state anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just bear with me for a second, because my colleague just informed me that we have to check the transcript in terms of interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tubakovic, could you please tell me, if you remember, perhaps, in that period, whether criminal proceedings were initiated against the volunteers Crni, Lugar, and the others before the military Tribunal in Banja Luka. Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that before that, they - and I cannot remember exactly when - I know that they were arrested. Whether that was then or later, or whether there were any criminal proceedings initiated at all, to tell you the truth, I really wasn't informed about this. Because after a while - and again, I say this was a long time ago - we found out that they were released; they were free. This is what I remember happening. Whether there were any criminal proceedings and they were released or acquitted, I really don't know. Perhaps there weren't any proceedings at all. It wasn't in the command -- up to the command, or it wasn't our job to receive any information relating to this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. On page 230 of the transcript of the depositions that were conducted in Belgrade, at the end of your testimony, the Prosecutor asked you a whole series of questions relating to the alleged participation of the civilian authorities in certain incidents, failings, criminal acts, and so on. Since the Defence at the time could not object to the manner of questioning because of the relevant instructions and rulings by the Trial Chamber, one of their questions was --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object to that. That's simply not the case. Mr. -- the Trial Chamber's rulings did not prevent other Defence objecting to my submission to evidence being given. The ruling prevented them cross-examining. It didn't prevent them putting an objection on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, and objections were being made by counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In any case, Mr. Tubakovic, the Prosecutor, amongst other questions, asked you whether this information that was compiled in the brigade was actually out of concern about what the civilian authorities were doing with the prisoners, this isolation, unfounded arrests, looting, and so on. Since this is quite a broad term, would you agree with me if I were to tell you that the police actually were in charge of the arrest and detention procedures? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I completely agree with you, because I don't know who else would be the executor of such matters if not the civilian police, which was given the task of establishing law and order, conditionally speaking, but it actually committed some acts with which the command did not agree, and this is why it reacted by compiling this information document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tubakovic, the Prosecutor then asked you if the concern of the command regarding discrimination against members of other ethnic groups in Samac was also the reason for compiling this document, and the Prosecutor actually linked that with the civilian authorities. But I would like you now to tell the Trial Chamber the following: When you were replying to the questions by the Prosecution, and when the term "civilian authorities" was used in the questions, what did you actually think of? Which institution or which circle of officials did you mean when you confirmed for the Prosecutor their claims? Could you please explain that to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I mostly meant the public security station or the police, the civilian police, which actually implemented these activities that were carried out, with which the command or the military did not agree, and that is why, conditionally speaking, it lodged a protest by issuing this information. Because I don't know who else could have carried out these unlawful activities if not armed people. And in this case, they were not members of the military but members of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Tubakovic, would you agree with me that in that period, during the wartime period in Samac, that there were some individual acts of looting, but there was no looting which was organised by the political organs or by any other body? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that that is a realistic claim that there were -- I don't think that it was the position of any institution or political authority to commit looting. I think that this was something that was done by individuals. But those who were supposed to prevent that perhaps did not do that, but that again, in my opinion, is the police. I don't know, I'm not informed about it, but I don't know that there was a position by any of the institutions of authority or political organs to commit looting. I don't think that something like that happened. But there were individual instances of looting. It was widely known that there was looting, and this was something that the police should have prevented, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I've finished with the cross-examination of this witness. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Tubakovic. I have completed my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Tubakovic, good morning. I'm going to ask you a few questions --

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- following on from the questions we asked you in Belgrade and the things Mr. Pantelic has just asked you about. You arrived here yesterday; is that correct, from -- sorry, the day before, from Bosanski Samac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- you of course had a conference with Mr. Pisarevic and Mr. Lazarevic, who called you; you spoke to them about coming to the Trial Chamber and giving your evidence, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And tell me: Last night, did you have a conference or talk to Mr. Pantelic about your evidence or speak to him about what you might be saying in court today?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Last night, Mr. Pisarevic, myself, and then Mr. Pantelic came later, we sat down for a while. They told me how things will proceed here generally, and yes, that is what we talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want to ask you specifically: Did you and Mr. Pantelic discuss what you were going to talk about, that is, the evidence you gave in Belgrade and the sorts of things that he was going to ask you about when you came to court today?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: We talked a little bit, but we didn't actually discuss any of those questions which he put to me just now. That was not discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you talk about the areas, the sort of topics, not the specific questions but the topics, such as the document you signed, the one you and the other command members signed, which is the one in evidence here? Did you talk about in general what you were going to talk about?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly what I said: Generally, there was talk about the topics that he would ask me about, but not the specific things that he asked me now. Generally, we discussed that he would put to me questions relating to the information that we adopted, but not specifically the questions that he put to me just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was one of the things he raised that looting was one of the things you were -- he was going to be talking about, but not the specific question, but the general area of looting?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't mention looting at all last night. That was not discussed at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about who was actually carrying out the arrest? Did you talk about -- did you and Mr. Pantelic talk about, in any general sense, who was actually carrying out the arrests in Samac, whether it was the police or the military, in a general sense?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did talk about that. That was discussed. There was a kind of clarification regarding that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. And what about the meeting which occurred a few days after you prepared the report, the meeting in Pelagicevo, which Dr. Simic attended? Did -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want to ask you: Did you and Mr. Pantelic talk about in a general sense what Dr. Simic said or what happened at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't ask me about what Dr. Simic said at that meeting. Mr. Pantelic didn't ask me that. We discussed the looting [as interpreted]. We spoke very briefly, perhaps two or three minutes, about those topics. There wasn't really much talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We have some clarification here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The witness said we didn't discuss the looting and here it says we did discuss the looting, on page 11, line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I thought I heard that we didn't. It's the recording which is wrong, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll just clarify that with you. Did you say you discussed the looting or didn't discuss the looting? There's something a little bit unclear here?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't discuss about the looting last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Actually, it was quite clear on line 8 of page 11, where the witness specifically said that, that he didn't discuss that, so it's already there on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was just clarifying the last answer for the record, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And a moment ago, when I asked you about arrests in general, you said we did talk about that. That was discussed. There was a kind of clarification regarding that topic. Just tell us in broad terms what the clarification regarding the topic was that you discussed with Mr. Pantelic last night.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: The clarification was as follows: Mr. Pantelic asked me who were the people who implemented those acts, and I said the same thing to him that I told you just now. I said that that was the police. I don't know who else it could have been. The police, the civilian police. This was something that was discussed a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you a deputy or a member of either the assembly elected in October 1990 or the Serbian Samac Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was a deputy in the multiparty assembly, one of the deputies. I think there were 50 deputies in the assembly. The first multiparty assembly in Samac. And I was one of them. The assembly was constituted, as you said, I don't remember very well, but I think it was in late 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what about the Serbian Municipal Assembly, that was the Samac one from February or March 1992? Were you a member of that one, or a deputy?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As an elected deputy, elected at the multiparty elections which were held, I think, in 1989 or 1990, I was elected a deputy. And while the multiparty assembly was still functioning, I was a deputy in it. I continued on as a deputy of the Serbian Assembly of Samac. That's what it was called. I remember now. Yes, yes. I was a deputy there too, because I just continued. There was a continuum.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you -- did you run on the SDS platform when you were elected to the 1990 -- sorry, in the 1990 elections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Maybe -- we have bad interpretation. We just heard that there were elections from 1999 or something. Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think just repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you ran for the assembly in the 1990 elections, did you run on the SDS platform as a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The SDS platform, yes, which I studied thoroughly at that time, and this was my political option.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you remain a member of the SDS throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did you leave the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, how shall I put it? When I think about it now, I was a deputy and a member of the SDS. But when the war broke out and everything that happened, happened, I came to understand that what was happening was not in line with the SDS platform, and I had the impression that these things were being implemented under cover of the SDS, so I simply withdrew from that political structure. I don't know whether my answer was clear enough, but I hope it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could you clarify -- could you maybe expand on that and clarify sort of things that you say were being implemented under the cover of the SDS? What do you mean by that? What sort of things?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout 1989, 1990, up to the elections, the national feelings, not only Serb national feelings - I think the Serbs were the last to organise themselves - but there was also the Muslim and the Croatian national feelings, so the vast majority of the population grouped to themselves, so to speak. And at the multiparty elections, the national parties won the vast majority of votes. However, due to the course of events, because we are now discussing the SDS platform, and in that platform and the regulations that were officially adopted, there was a statement, or a provision, that any citizen could be a member of the SDS who accepted the platform and the statute, regardless of their ethnicity. So it wasn't only for the Serbs. Nowhere in the platform was there any ethnic intolerance, because had there been something like that, I would not have opted for that party, if you understand me. However, this did begin to emerge in practice later on, and when I recall all these events now, it was very difficult to speak out publicly against the practices that were being implemented. Because as the war went on, especially in the autumn of 1992, when a certain number of so-called Specials, or volunteers, arrived, who intimidated all of us, one could not fight for democratic options in public, and that is why I silently withdrew. I did not wish to be a participant in such activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A moment ago you mentioned -- there was nothing in the platform about ethnic intolerance. Are you saying one of your concerns, one of the reasons you left the SDS, silently, was your concern of the ethnic intolerance and the way they were implementing policies, hidden policies of ethnic intolerance?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so, yes, but it wasn't just the SDS. The same thing happened with the other national parties. The SDS was not a political organisation creating ethnic intolerance. The SDA and the HDZ were doing the same. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And are you saying that your concern was you noticed or you saw that all of the parties were promoting or were engaging in ethnic intolerance, leading to ethnic cleansing of various areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And that was something you experienced in Samac, the SDS's involvement in ethnic cleansing in the Samac municipality, and was that one of the reasons why you left the SDS in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, because of the overall course of events and all the negative things that were happening, which -- well, this was mentioned as something the SDS was doing. I simply withdrew because I didn't want to have anything to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just asking you specifically about Samac and what you saw there. I'm asking you: Is that something you saw, the ethnic cleansing by the SDS in the Samac municipality, which was your home area? Was that something you saw and concerned or distressed you, causing you to leave the party?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what is now called "ethnic cleansing" was not defined as such at the time, and because of the ethnic intolerance that had already been prevailing for a year or two and given rise to the war, due to circumstances, wherever one ethnic option prevailed and set up its own government, the others moved away. And so in Samac, it happened that the Serb national option took over power, and then the Croats and the Muslims, or the Bosniaks, as they call themselves now, they started leaving. As far as I can remember, people could hardly wait to leave the territory. Of course, with hindsight, it all looks very different now. I did not understand at the time that the aim of what was happening was to ethnically cleanse a certain territory. I wouldn't say that the SDS, as an organised political structure of the time -- let me repeat: It never officially adopted the position that ethnic cleansing should be carried out. This was not the case. I think it was a tacit policy. I didn't like it, and so I left the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But that's exactly the effect of what happened in Samac, wasn't it, as a result of SDS policies and the way they were pursued in that area? It was ethnically cleansed of non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, very well. When we look at it now, from this point of time, that's how it appears. There's nothing else I can add. But at the time, it seemed to be something else. People wanted to go to their own ethnic milieus. But now it's defined as ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But sir, you know that a lot of people didn't leave voluntarily, a lot of people were arrested, as you've already described, and locked up and exchanged, and their exchange wasn't voluntary on their part and that was one of the reasons why a lot of people left your municipality, wasn't it, because they had no choice?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is being asked to speculate as to whether these people left voluntarily or not. He should be asked whether he himself personally had knowledge, as a witness, as to whether they were forced to leave or whether they left voluntarily. Whether he has any direct knowledge of this. He should not be asked to speculate as to why they left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In my submission, the witness can answer the question. He's already given evidence about people leaving. I'm suggesting that this was the reason. He can agree, he can disagree, or he can say something else. I'm not asking him to speculate. If he knows, he knows; if he doesn't know, he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The witness was living in the area and he can give the answers according to the information that he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I was asking you a moment ago, the question was: You are aware that a lot of people didn't leave voluntarily. The document you signed, you talked -- the document talks about the arrests of people, the isolation of people, and people were locked up and exchanged, and that process meant that they weren't leaving voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. I agree that these measures were taken and that these people were mistreated, isolated, arrested, detained, locked up, and so on. And this increased their wish to leave. And of course, under pressure and wishing to escape from these misfortunes, they left. That is logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And from what you're saying, logically, that's what you, in hindsight, now, describe as one -- describe as part of the ethnic cleansing, isn't it, that process?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I say that's the term used now, "ethnic cleansing," so we have to accept it. But at the time, we never thought of that kind of terminology. I never noticed it at the time. But I did see what was happening and that people were leaving, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm just seeking to clarify is, when you said you agreed that people were mistreated, et cetera, and this increased their wish to leave, and of course under pressure they -- and wishing to escape from these misfortunes, they left, that's logical. What I'm suggesting is that was the sort of thing that you're now describing with hindsight with the new word of ethnic cleansing. What you just talked about was actually part of the ethnic cleansing, the locking up and the isolation and getting people to the point where they wished to leave or they had to leave, with hindsight, that's the word which could have been used at the time but it used now.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Tubakovic, you were a member of the 4th Detachment, were you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was never a member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your evidence, when you gave the deposition evidence in Belgrade, was of your joining the VRS in May of 1992. What were you doing between early April and mid-May?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think I said this in Belgrade. I was, starting in October, I think, 1991, as an officer of the JNA. I was assigned to the wartime assignment of commander of the 2nd Detachment of the 17th Tactical Group, and I remained in that post until the 19th of May, 1992, when, under the decision issued by I think the assembly or the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the federal government of the time, the JNA had to withdraw from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the JNA left, or rather, the officers who had been born in Serbia, Montenegro, and other republics outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, left Bosnia and Herzegovina and only those officers who remained took over the command, and these originated from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was then a member of the command of the 17th Tactical Group, which is renamed the 2nd Posavina Brigade, and I was a member of the command of that brigade, starting from the 19th of May, 1992 until the 7th of July, 1993, when I went to Bijeljina, to the engineering regiment, and at the request of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Specifically, where were you on the 16th and 17th of April, 1992, when Samac -- the town of Bosanski Samac was taken over?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: The 16th and the 17th, whether I was at home in Samac or at my command post -- I think I was at the command post, because I was a commander of the 2nd Detachment. And if you're speaking of the night between the 16th and the 17th, I was at home. But in the morning I went to my command, in the early morning, at about 7.00 a.m. and my command post was in Crkvina, the village of Crkvina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what orders did you receive on the morning of the 17th, and what did you and your detachment actually do on the morning or the day of the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 17th, in the morning, I received an order that the entire detachment should be called up, and this was done during the day, mobilisation was carried out, and I was given the task to secure the right bank of the River Bosna from the boundary of Modrica municipality to the right bank of the River Bosna up to the territory belonging to the town of Samac. So I was to secure the right bank of the River Bosna and control the territory towards the villages of Hasici. These villages were in the area of responsibility of my detachment. The right bank of the River Bosna and, to the south, the villages of Gornji and Donji Hasici. That was my assignment, and I carried it out successfully after the mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want a name here. Who gave you those orders?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 17th Tactical Group, Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic, gave me this command. I was directly subordinate to him. My detachment was an integral part of that Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want a one-word answer, if possible. Was it a written or an oral order Colonel Nikolic gave you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was by telephone, by radio, and the command came from the 17th Tactical Group, to mobilise the detachment and to deploy it along the line I have already described.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did Colonel Nikolic tell you who had given him those orders or why he was giving you those orders?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. He had no reason to do that. He was my superior officer, so he was not accountable to me. He just gave me the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The answer is quite clear, but maybe, what we heard as the translation of the question is: Why Colonel Nikolic received such orders. This is what we heard as translation. This is what we heard. But I believe that the answer of the witness was quite clear, that he didn't discuss this with Colonel Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I don't see anything to repeat here. I think we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: This deployment along the banks of the River Bosna, was that directly facing Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. The River Bosna does not run along the border with the Republic of Croatia. It's the River Sava that runs along the border with the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise. That was my mistake, sir. I'll move along. When you -- sorry. Did Colonel Nikolic order you or your detachment to participate in weapons searches in the areas in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think yes, but not on that day. In the area of responsibility of my battalion, or rather, my detachment, on the bank of the River Bosna, there was a small Croatian village called Zasavica, and as it was right by the river, later on I was given the task to contact the representatives of the Zasavica local commune, and this was two or three days after the 17th, I can't remember the exact date. Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic told me to talk to the representatives of the local commune, and if they had any military weapons, that they should hand them over to the battalion command. On several occasions, I talked to the representatives of the local commune, and they agreed to do this. They had very few weapons, but what they had, they handed over, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll just stop you for a moment. I've just got to check something here. I'll just take you back to Crkvina, Mr. Tubakovic.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your troops were along the banks near Zasavica. Were your troops the 2nd Detachment, or any other troops actually stationed in Zasavica from the 17th of April onwards?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: In Zasavica, on the bank of the Bosna, near Zasavica, it was only my units that were there. No other units. On that territory, it was I alone, and no one else was given the task of securing the River Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And how many people did you have securing the River Bosna? Just the number if possible, please. How long did you stay there? Two things: How many people and how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Securing the River Bosna was a task that continued from then onwards, without interruption. From the border of Modrica up to the edge of the territory of Bosanski Samac. This was some three or four kilometres along the River Bosna, and there were about a hundred conscripts at any given time, and they, of course, changed. They were relieved from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the report which the members of the Posavina Brigade prepared, which is called P127 in these proceedings, you refer to the arrival of a paramilitary group or Serbian commandos, in a helicopter. It's all right. I'm just --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have no problem, but maybe if you are referring to the document, maybe the witness should have it before him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course he should, but what I'm saying is just a very, very general thing. Can the witness please be given the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In the document you refer to the arrival of Serbian commandos and paramilitaries. What I'm asking you, without needing to look at the document, is simply this: Were any of those people deployed with your detachment along the banks of the River Bosna at any time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody was deployed from my detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your answer just was: Nobody was deployed from my detachment. What I'm -- maybe that was a slight error in translation.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, none of those para -- I understood the question to say whether those who arrived, the paramilitary units, those who arrived from Serbia, whether they were deployed in my detachment. No, none of them was deployed in my detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I put it another way? Did your detachment ever work, ever do any -- were you ever involved in any operations jointly with those special -- with the -- what you've described as -- it's all right. I'm not actually referring to the document. It's only general. You can -- Madam Usher, you can sit down. The Serbian commandos or the paramilitary group, were any of -- did your group -- did your detachment ever involve -- ever engage in any operations with them, at any time after their arrival?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. My detachment did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was your detachment involved in the operation to clear the road to Brcko on the 8th of - can I just finish the question - 8th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I can just make a principled objection. This witness testified during the depositions in Belgrade, and regarding his testimony in chief, and it is known what he testified about while giving his deposition, I think the Prosecutor had about an hour to ask him about these topics. The purpose of him arriving here today is to allow the other Defence members to cross-examine him on matters which arose out of the questions from his deposition. Mr. Pantelic put certain questions to him, and now I understand that the only task of the Prosecution is not to be given an additional hour to ask about the things which were not put to the witness during the deposition but to provide them with the opportunity to clarify things that arise from the testimony now. I object to the Prosecution being given another chance to put questions that they failed to put the first time. The Prosecutor is putting new topics to the witness and things that arose throughout the whole trial, and I think that it is not fair that the Prosecutor be allowed to put new questions about topics which they did not put at the proper time, are now being given the opportunity to open up new topics. I think that they are being given additional time outside of the framework of the deposition, and I don't think that that was the gist of the decision of the Trial Chamber, and that was the original purpose was to allow the Defence to put questions which might pertain to their clients.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, the motion was quite specific. The motion was to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Re. I think there is a misunderstanding here by Mr. Lukic. This is not a continuation of the deposition process. When the motion was put to the Trial Chamber, the gist was that this witness -- or that this witness had -- it appeared that he had more information or he was capable of giving more evidence on the issues in the indictment, not necessarily what he stated at the deposition level. So this is why the Trial Chamber ordered that he come, and if parties wish to elicit whatever evidence they want to elicit from him, they could do so, and that is why everybody was given the limited period of one hour to do so. So it -- his evidence here is not to be limited to what was discussed during the deposition process.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for this interpretation, and in that case, I cannot put my objection. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I just check LiveNote to find out -- I can't remember what my last question was, Your Honour. I've just got to check the computer on the side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tubakovic. My question was a moment ago: Was your detachment or were you involved in the operation to clear the road to Brcko on the 8th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. My detachment had the task that it had, and that task remained in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Similarly, you weren't involved, then, in the clearing of the road to Modrica on the 10th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It would be fair to say that the document which you have there, P127, is critical of Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic. If you'd just go to the first page, where it says -- perhaps it's the first page. It would be the third paragraph, where it says: Second. Even while Tactical Group 17 existed and Lieutenant Nikolic was here. Have you just found that portion?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm saying: It's a fair conclusion that the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, of which you were one of the signatories of this document, was critical of the role Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic had after the arrival of these Serbian commandos or paramilitaries from Serbia. Or I'm sorry, or from wherever they came.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: The command was not critical towards Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic, because he was the commander of the Tactical Group. We were somewhat surprised with the departure of all the senior officers who came originally from Serbia, by the fact that they left the command, but that was their legal right. So I think, as far as I remember, we were critical towards that. We noted that they had actually left suddenly, even though we knew about that -- the term that the JNA, as an armed force, was being dismantled that, that it wasn't functioning any more, and that is why they left. We expressed a general small criticism because they left and they didn't stay. That is what we did. But we didn't have any objections against him as a commander, or against his work as a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's not quite what I'm asking you. I just want you to look at that paragraph, and it says -- the second sentence: "Nikolic and the 17th Tactical Group command initially branded it as a `paramilitary group' and a `group of bandits and mercenaries,' but after only five or six days, they endorsed it and explained it as a `legal elite of Serbian commandos,' whose arrival had been legalised through the official organs of government and the army, both at the level of Samac municipality and at the highest level in Serbia." You see what I've just read out to you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where you say there "they endorsed it and explained it," I just want you to expand on what your understanding of their endorsement is in this document. But please, as briefly as you can.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: It states here that after a couple of days after their arrival, five to six days, the same, and that is -- I assume that this refers to the fact that probably Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic consulted his Superior Command and received some kind of explanation that this was a group which had come at the invitation of either the public security station of the police, but did not come at the invitation of the military, and that this is how I'm interpreting it now, that I -- that this group was being accepted by the civilian -- the public security station and that the army should not interfere in this in any way. This is how I am understanding it now, as I am reading it. Five to six interpreted as the -- that would be that. I assume that that is that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you -- were you aware of Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic using these men under the command of Lugar and Crni for the -- for various operations, and they being subordinated to his command?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. They were not subordinated to his command. As far as I know, this was not anywhere. They were not subordinated. They were not part of the Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. I'm not suggesting they were part of the Tactical Group. But what I'm saying: Are you aware -- and there's evidence before the Trial Chamber of this, of Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic using them for various operations. I'm just asking were you, as Major Tubakovic, aware that Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic was using them in specific operations and subordinating them to him for those specific operations? That's all I'm asking. If you can't remember, that's perfectly okay.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of him using them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In that document, these people are described as "Serbian commandos" led by Crni and Debeli, or a paramilitary group. Where were you told that they had come from and who they were?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody explained anything to me or was obliged to do so, but I heard, like everyone else, that this was a group that arrived from Serbia, that they were Special Forces, some kind of Special Forces, and that they would be under the authority of the police. That is what we heard. This was the story that we got, and this is how things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anything about them being part of the Krajina police?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There is something in the interpretation. When -- and it is just some sort of -- it is not actually a mistake in the translation, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- Krajina, we also have the Krajina Corps, and we have -- and the way it was translated in B/C/S, it might suggest that it was police in Krajina Corps or something like that. So maybe you should use "Serbian Krajina in Croatia," Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have limited time. I'm trying to get to the point quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My question is this. Did you ever hear anything about them being police from Krajina, however interpreted?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. I heard that they came from Serbia, but I don't know who they belonged to. I didn't know it at the time either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You gave evidence in Belgrade, gave some deposition evidence, specifically at page 224 of the depositions, where I asked you about the document in the meeting, and I said: "What did Blagoje Simic say to the meeting about the report?" It's not in there. It's in the transcript of what you said in Belgrade. It was written down.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your answer was: "It wasn't only Blagoje. All of them sought -- tried to negate what we had highlighted as negative practices, negative trends within the zone of responsibility." I just want to ask you simply this, and if you can answer it yes, please do so. You stand by the evidence you gave when I asked you those questions in Belgrade, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you also stand by the question I asked you at page 225: "I just want you to concentrate for a moment on Blagoje Simic. What do you remember him saying at the meeting?" Answer -- this is your answer: "Well, probably something along the lines of what the other people were saying, that he didn't agree to us having done that. I cannot remember details. I know that they were displeased at what we had written." All I'm asking you again is: You stand by that question and answer that you gave to me in Belgrade, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and also I am augmenting it with what I have just said, because I remembered some other things, some other things I recalled, I spoke about them, so I remembered more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course. That's completely normal, Mr. Tubakovic. And also, of course, you stand by this question and answer. Question, page 225, the next one: "Was their concern the fact that the military had written this report about what the civilians were doing rather than it was what the civilians were doing?" I'm saying was their concern the fact that you, the military, had written this, do you live follow what I'm saying? And your answer was: "Yes, yes, exactly. That was it precisely. We gained the impression that they resented the fact that it was us analysing the situation in this area, the situation among the population. They said it's up to you. Yours is to take care of the army, of the military issues, and it's up to see -- up to see what is happening amongst the civilian population." That's it. Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And this report you wrote, that's the one you have there, do you remember ever talking to your brother Djordje Tubakovic about the report or the fact that you had written the report, expressing the command's concerns about the Crisis Staff or War Presidency and what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I talked to my brother when I returned from Belgrade. We did have a conversation very soon afterwards. He asked me why did I go to Belgrade. So I explained to him briefly what the topic of my testimony was in Belgrade, and that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Slight misunderstanding. I mean at the time you wrote the report and the time surrounding the report, November, December 1992, January 1993, do you remember talking to him about the report or your concerns about -- that is your, the Posavina --

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. No. I didn't discuss that with anyone, not with anyone, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the War Presidency, or the Crisis Staff, were you aware of a military representative being on the War Presidency or the Crisis Staff, and if so, if you're aware of it, who was the representative of the military?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who the military representative was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's just one final issue, one final question I wish to ask you, a very short topic. I just want to -- you gave evidence earlier about looting. You said something to Mr. Pantelic about it. I just want to tell you what Mr. Zaric said in his interview to the Prosecutor on the 2nd of April, 1998. That's P141 and it's at page 94 of the ter version. I'll just read you briefly what it says and ask you whether you agree with it. The Prosecutor, that's Nancy said: "So this is the Samac Crisis Staff who was allowing this looting to go on?" To which Mr. Zaric answered: "Yes. Many things were taken away. It was all organised by them. Many things were hidden from me. I don't know where things were taken, but I know that many things were taken then." That's what Mr. Zaric said in his interview to the Prosecutor in 1998. Do you agree with what he said there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who organised the looting. I know that there was looting. I saw that, just like any other citizens. I saw that there was looting. Whether this was organised by anyone or whether this was spontaneous looting, I don't know, whether to say that it was one or the order. But I don't know that the Crisis Staff adopted a decision on looting. Perhaps it did, but I don't know. But it was a fact that there was looting. That is something that I agree with.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the end of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Any matters arising that counsel wish to clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I just wanted to clarify something with the witness that arose from the questions and that pertains to the defence of my client.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tubakovic, I'm Novak Lukic, counsel for Mr. Tadic. I just have a couple of questions in response to the questions asked you by the Prosecutor regarding the responsibility and the people who were leaving Samac, and he said whether -- if somebody was exchanged, and then later -- if somebody was arrested and then later was exchanged, would they be forced to go? And you responded -- actually, in that context, you mentioned the exchange. My first question is as follows: Did -- were you, Mr. Tubakovic, present at any exchange at the very place of the exchange?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was not present there. This was not something that was done by the military, so I didn't have such a task or the opportunity to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know when you were replying to the Prosecutor, did you know that at the line where the exchange was carried out, all of those who were brought for the exchange stated whether they wanted to cross over to the other side or not? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I did have some knowledge about that, and that is why I said that people wanted to go, because the situation was such. Whether this desire stemmed from some kind of compulsion or some desire, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question is specific: Did you know whether people said, when they were at the place of exchange, whether they wanted to go or not?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I was never at the line of exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you were responding to the Prosecutor, did you know, were you aware of the fact that the people who were detained and who were taken to an exchange but did not wish to go to the exchange, they could go home, they could choose whether they could go home, they actually went back home, they didn't go back to gaol? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that we heard testimony here about how people on the line, people who were detained in Samac and Batkovic were able to say at the line that they did not want to go across and that they were allowed to go back home and that they're living in Samac still today, if I were to tell you that, would you reconsider your response to the Prosecutor whether people considered whether they wanted to go voluntarily or not?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't participate in that activity, so I accept what are the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one small -- oh, yes. Very well. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tubakovic, the Prosecutor asked you about your party affiliation this morning. Could you please tell me: When you became a soldier, did you continue to work in politics or did you stop?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I stopped with that. I wasn't thinking about politics, and I began to carry out the tasks that were entrusted to me by the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the fact that in 1992 and 1993, the activities of political parties in Republika Srpska were frozen?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that that was true. As far as I recall now --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object. The purpose of Mr. Pantelic being permitted to recross-examine is if there's anything that affected the interests of his client from my cross-examination that he didn't cover himself earlier. This is, in my respectful submission, outside the scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If I recall, the Prosecution did ask questions regarding the practices of the SDS and the witness did give answers as to how he left the SDS, so I think it's quite related.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's absolutely correct, Your Honour. That was also my understanding, and therefore I'm pursuing this line of questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tubakovic, could you please tell me: Do you have any personal knowledge about Dr. Blagoje Simic in the period from the autumn of 1991 until the end of 1993 personally promoting ethnic intolerance, ethnic hate, policies of expulsion, and so on? Do you know anything like that about Dr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. I don't have any such knowledge about him. In my presence, that was something that I never heard, so I cannot have any knowledge about it if I never heard anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It is now time for a break, but we have time for one brief question. Did you ever hear anybody say that Dr. Blagoje was supporting such a policy?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, appropriate time for our break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take our break at this time and continue at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: For the sake of clarity, we'll go back to our normal break time. This time we shall continue for an hour, have a break at 12.30, resume at 12.50, up to 1345 hours, and then continue in the afternoon at 1445. Yes, Mr. Pantelic. You still have questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I believe one or two, so I will finish in a couple of minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tubakovic, to the Prosecutor's question in connection with the comments on this information in the part relating to the JNA, I have a question to put to you. After the 19th of May, 1992, were there any JNA officers in the 2nd Posavina Brigade who originated from Serbia? I'm referring to them.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of May, 1992, JNA officers who had been born outside the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina left our command. As far as I can remember, none of them remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The military cadres, were they composed of local conscripts or were there also conscripts from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Both the officers and the privates who were born outside Bosnia-Herzegovina were duty-bound to leave the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina on that date, so that only the local population remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You mean from the Samac area?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the area of Samac, Pelagicevo, the territory of the area of responsibility of the 2nd Posavina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tubakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... thank you, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tubakovic. I just have a few questions, four, to be exact

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: First of all, this morning, page 8, lines 2 to 3 of the transcript, Mr. Pantelic asked you a question concerning the police being in charge of arrests and detention, and on line 4 of page 8, you agreed with that. You recall that, Mr. Tubakovic? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course I remember. I heard, I saw. I saw little, but I heard a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So my question, actual question to you is: Do you have any knowledge as to which body or institution, if you like, if any, authorised the police to arrest and detain persons in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I have already said that I didn't hear from anyone, nor did I see, any official decision by any organ in connection with those tasks. I assume that they did this on their own initiative. I can only assume that. I can't be certain. Because had an organ of some sort issued such decisions, I would probably have heard about it by now, but I'm not aware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that answer. So my second question is concerning something you said in your deposition, Rule 71 evidence, and you mentioned - and this is on page 219 of the transcript of that testimony - you mentioned, in answer to a question by Mr. Pisarevic concerning P127, the 13 signatories document, that -- sorry, page 218 of that document, of the transcript, you mentioned that the report was not to be mentioned, that mentioning that any such report existed was not part of the plan, if you like - that's my word - of the members of the command. So I'm wondering: If this document was to be kept confidential, what was its purpose, if it was going to be kept as a confidential document?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that I explained this in Belgrade, but I'll try again. The brigade command, on several occasions, discussed the negative occurrences that were leading to a decline in the morale of the army of Republika Srpska, and in the end, drew up the information, the document you now have. This was adopted at a meeting of the command, and I have just seen that it was, I think, on the 29th of November, 1992. The members of the command adopted it unanimously, and their conclusion was that the text of the document, of the information, should be for the information of the members of the command, so that they could continue to act in order to raise morale, in order to try to act, each within his own sphere of competence within the 2nd Posavina Brigade, in order to remove the negative phenomena mentioned in the document, in the information. The information as such was to be archived in the command and not to be used or even mentioned as existing. We were not supposed to go to the units and say: Well, you know, we've conducted an analysis. We've collected information and read out the document. The information was simply to be used in order to improve the situation. How it came about that it was leaked to the public, I have no idea. I assume the commander had to have done it, because no other member of the command could have done that or would have dared to do that, or wanted to do it. I assume that the content of the information reached the structures of the civilian government, and I assume it did so through the commander. It certainly wasn't through me, and I assume it wasn't through any other member of the command. I don't know whether I have been clear enough and whether I have responded to your question. Was that what you wanted to learn?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarified some things that were in my mind. But one thing you mentioned here in that respect is that this document was therefore an internal - that's my word, internal command document - and a confidential document, as we know, and that it was then the intention was simply to archive it. Now, what that sort of raises in my mind is: How could the situation in Bosanski Samac, the tensions, these negative tendencies that are mentioned in connection with the civilian authorities and so on, how could the situation be ameliorated if such a document was simply intended to be put in the archives of the command?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat: The document, as a piece of paper that had been signed, was to be kept in the archives and was not to be used as such, saying that the command adopted the document on such-and-such a date. However, the contents of the document were to be borne in mind by the members of the command in their attempts to ameliorate the situation. We were to go to the units, and we could say we know that such-and-such things have happened, how can we improve the situation, how can we remove the negative tendencies? We weren't to go and say: We have conducted an analysis, collected information, we are acting on this basis. So we were to use the information contained in the document, but not show the document itself. That was what the conclusion of the command was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And in fact my last question concerns once again something you said in your deposition evidence, and this is at the top of page 229. And you mention -- I'll just read the sentence. It says: "The control and command system was, of course, from the command of the brigade up to the command of the corps and the Main Staff, but the civilian authorities could exert an influence on the army via the commander because he succumbed to such." And then it goes on and says: "Because formerly they were not entitled to interfere in what were the terms of reference of the brigade command." So I'm just interested in knowing what you meant by the words "but the civilian authorities could exert an influence on the army via the commander, because he succumbed to such."

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: Direct contacts with the civilian authorities, that was something that every member of the command had in connection with his own sphere of competence. The commander was the embodiment of the command, the personification of the command, and he was in possession of the powers he had. How he cooperated, in what area, and what talks he had with the representatives of the authorities, that's something he knows. I don't know that. I was simply a member of the command. It's possible, and I'm speculating now, it's possible that, and I assume that the information reached the civilian authorities through the commander. I can only assume that. I can't be certain. He's the one who knows that. It wasn't done through me. So I assume that in his conversations with individuals that were in the civilian authorities, he adopted certain suggestions made to him by those authorities, but he was not duty-bound to do so, because in any military in the world, there is a chain of command that has nothing to do with the civilian authorities. Whether he succumbed to them, as I said, he probably did, probably. But I can't be certain, because I wasn't there, so that I can't be certain. He may have accepted some suggestions that he shouldn't have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I apologise. I said that was the last one, but I have one now that just follows on from what you've said. To your knowledge - and if you don't know, obviously just say that right away - did the civilian authorities in the municipality of Bosanski Samac in any way influence a decision of Lieutenant Commander Nikolic to instruct Commander Antic and Mr. Zaric, as persons in the command of the 4th Detachment, not to intervene directly in the situation of the takeover in Bosanski Samac, but solely to be on the alert and take up defensive positions, notably along the river embankments between the municipality and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that was the task of the 4th Detachment, and it had no other tasks. Just as my task was to secure the River Bosna and nothing else. In the same way, they were given this task. I don't know the details of it, because I wasn't in that command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So the question simply put: To your knowledge, did the civilian authorities, the Crisis Staff or any other part of the authorities in Bosanski Samac, influence the decision of Colonel -- Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic to instruct the 4th Detachment in the way he did? And as I said, if you don't know, simply say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MARKO TUBAKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that they didn't, but it's better to say that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much for those answers and clarifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I notice from the transcript that before Judge Williams started asking questions, I hadn't asked Mr. Pisarevic or Mr. Lazarevic whether they wanted to clarify anything out of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. We didn't have any re-examination. Otherwise, I would raise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Tubakovic. We have finished with you. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We will continue with Mr. Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Is the technical equipment functioning?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we were talking about the arrival of members of the military police in a truck in Pinzgauers and so on, and you explained how a military truck with a canvas cover entered the courtyard of the Territorial Defence staff. Do you remember that that's the last topic we talked about?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please: What happened after this? Did you, Mr. Zaric, then enter the courtyard and the premises of the Territorial Defence, where detainees were held?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone else enter the premises with you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Makso Simeunovic did. He arrived with the vehicles and the military police escort, and Mr. Mihajlo Topolovac came in likewise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you enter the room where the detainees were, and if you did, how did you do that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I entered the room because the guard who was in charge of guarding the facility opened a room, and this was the first and only time I entered that room during the whole time of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When the guard opened the door to this room where the detainees were held in the TO staff, what did you see? Can you tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my estimation, the room was perhaps some 50 square metres in area. In the centre of that room there is a wooden pillar, a weight-bearing pillar. On that wooden pillar there was a metal tin containing sand, and there was a candle there which was lighted. At that moment there were no electric lights in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And by the light of the candle, what did you see? How many people were there? What was their condition? And what impression did this leave on you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me, it was a terrible sight. I have to be quite sincere. The room was relatively small for the number of people inside it. In my estimation, there were between 40 and 50 people inside. I didn't count them, but that's my opinion, as far as I could judge at that moment. I would only like to say that the reflection of the candlelight from the candle burning on the pillar in the middle of the room fell on the faces of the people in the room, and what I could see were vague outlines. You couldn't clearly see people's faces. And also what I was able to see was so bad that I could hardly recognise those people. When I say that, I mean that many of them were unshaved, many were deformed from beatings, and even people standing quite close to me, I didn't recognise until they spoke to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you address those people, and how?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. This was a very unpleasant situation for me. Let me just add, in relation to the conditions: There was a very unpleasant odour in that room, and I couldn't understand how people could live in those conditions. It smelt of sweat, of urine, and various other smells were there. But it was something that was difficult to see, to look at, and only the people who were in that room can describe how they felt there. And I would also like to say something else about the conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wooden pillar, because I entered that room for the first time, it came right to the top of the ceiling, and there were wooden beams up there, and these were covered by planks, wooden planks. This means that the room in which the detainees were held did not have a concrete ceiling, so had a shell landed, by chance, on that room, because these were ordinary planks, there would have been a terrible tragedy. So this was what I saw, and I really want to tell the Chamber how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
