utterances.text: Thank you for this information. On the faces of those people, did you observe fear or anything else?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went in and I said: Good evening. I have to say that I was surprised, really, and it's up to the Chamber and the other participants whether they will believe me or not. They all got up as one and said, in unison: Good evening. I could see that there was a negative sort of discipline that had been drilled into them. So I assume when the Specials or the policemen who wanted to take it out on them came in, that's how they behaved. Because the moment I said "good evening," they all jumped up, almost standing to attention, one could say, and said "good evening," in unison, as one man.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did you tell them?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember my words very well. I said that I felt very uncomfortable at finding them in such a state, but this time I would not give a long speech. I need to tell you something quickly. Please relax and stand normally. I say that because they were standing in a stiff posture. I went on to say that within the military, it was agreed that they be transferred to a safer place so that we could spare them these conditions. And I said: Well, for the first time I am seeing where you are and how the places where you are, and I told them that they were being taken to a safer place, and I just said to them one thing: I would just like you to respect one discipline that I will indicate to you. At that point, from the depth of the room, a man called out whose voice I recognised later. That was Mr. Dragan Lukac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Dragan Lukac tell you then when he addressed you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First he told me: Mr. Zaric, Grga Zubak is asking you to speak to him. And I asked: And where is Grga? From the place where I was standing near this pillar, he was perhaps about two metres to the right, right next to the wall, and he was all bunched up, like a ball. He was in a crouching position. I went up to him, and please believe me, I couldn't recognise this person as Mr. Grga Zubak, because he was a completely deformed person. I couldn't believe that a live person could look so bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you say that he was all deformed, do you mean that the shape of his body was deformed?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His head was so swollen, it was bruised, black and blue. He could hardly speak because of his mouth. His eyes were completely closed, so that he just sensed me, because Mr. Grga recognised my voice and probably signaled to the others. I went up to Mr. Grga. I knelt next to him and I asked him: Grga, what do you want? The only two words that he uttered then were: Only if I had some water. That was the only thing that I could hear from him. And I must say that the stench from his mouth, because I came up very close to him, was really terrible, because he was all beaten up and bloodied. And I don't want to describe that scene now, but I told the guard: Bring water to this man. And after that, when I stood up, he asked me -- Mr. Dragan Lukac asked me again: Mr. Zaric, what will happen to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Zaric, what did you reply to Dragan Lukac and the others who were present there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told Mr. Lukac that I didn't have time for story telling but that we were doing everything through the military to transfer you to a safer place where you will be spared of all this abuse. At least, that's what I'm hoping. And then I more or less said the following: As far as you are concerned -- and then I saw the veterinarian standing next to him. He's quite a large man, so I noticed him. And then without thinking too much, I said: As far as you are concerned, and Dr. Ante, and also there was a Dr. Miroslav Keljacic, a doctor from Samac who was also there, and then Mr. Franjo Barukcic was standing right next to Grga. He was an elderly man from Samac who was born from Prud, and Sulejman Tihic. As far as all of you are concerned, I think that you are being treated as political prisoners and that things -- your questions will be resolved as soon as possible. And as far as all the others are concerned, I'm hoping that you will be freed as soon as possible. So these are the only things that I said at that point, before all of these 50 or so people, if there were so many, along with the presence of Mr. Simeunovic and Mr. Topolovac, who were standing right next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, could you please describe how the people were loaded up onto the truck. Were they called out? And if their names were called out, who was it who called out their names? How was it? What had happened?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that they all said thank you, in unison, and I said: Now, Mr. Mihajlo Topolovac will read this list to you, and I am asking you to get into the trucks as soon as possible so that we can leave here as soon as possible. After I said those words, I stepped back out of that room and I went almost to the end of the yard, towards the road, or towards the street that runs along that building, while Mr. Mihajlo Topolovac, and there was another police officer on duty with him, he was standing next to the trucks, and as the people were entering them, he was calling out their names and he was recording on a piece of paper that he had with him, the list. He was noting the names of the people who were entering the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you've said on two occasions that you were rushing and that you didn't have time. Why were you hurrying in this way in order to complete this task?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in my testimony yesterday that I had information that a group of Special Forces, headed by Mr. Todorovic and some of his police officers, were celebrating the Orthodox Easter in a cafe called Trile, which is several kilometres away from Samac. And that operative information was something that made me act immediately. It was my wish to do this as soon as possible, because I was afraid that Mr. Todorovic perhaps, or any of those other Special Forces who were prone to abusing people, wouldn't appear at that point, and then the whole procedure would be brought into question. That is why I wished to carry out this action as soon as possible, because besides all that I had said, within half an hour of everything, the trucks left for Brcko. That is how long the whole thing took.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So the people entered within half an hour. They were called out by Topolovac. Do you have any information about whether anyone remained in that room in the TO headquarters?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't go back any more, nor did I see anyone in that room. And just prior to the departure of the vehicles from the TO building, Mr. Sulejman Tihic was brought, as well as Mr. Ibrahim Salkic, who were at the premises of the public security station, and Safet Hadzialijagic was amongst the last to enter the bus [as interpreted] amongst all of those people. We called him Coner. He was one of the people who were in detention with the other detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. In transcript, it says they entered the bus, but they actually entered --

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They actually entered the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you saw Safet Hadzialijagic, aka Coner, did you say anything to him?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said something -- I must say, I forgot to say something when I said that I was going to say something to them about a certain type of discipline. I'm talking about all the detainees. I informed them, and I requested from them, that when they entered the vehicle, to be well-behaved and quiet. In front of the vehicle and behind the vehicle, there was a military police escort, and I didn't want any of them to decide to run from the truck and to bring into question this whole operation. And this person, Safet Hadzialijagic, aka Coner, when he entered the truck amongst the last of the people, I told him: Coner, please, what I asked you to do to prevent any problem from happening, please, could you take care of that? Because you're amongst the older people here. I know that this Coner enjoyed a certain authority amongst the people, and he told me: Simo, don't worry. There will be no problem. That was our last conversation before the trucks set off for Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And when Coner also entered the truck, did the column set out for Brcko?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One Pinzgauer was driving in front of the vehicles, in the middle was the truck, and then behind the truck there was the second Pinzgauer. And Mr. Makso Simeunovic was also there, but he had a special vehicle and a separate driver. And he went together with them, towards Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you follow this column that went towards Brcko?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Once they left in front of the building of the TO, I immediately said to Mr. Savo Cancarevic and Mihajlo Topolovac that I was going, and if anybody were to look for me, they could ask for me at the command. And that is why I left that place immediately, fearing that these people would come back and make trouble for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You said that these people wouldn't come back. Could you please clarify. Who do you mean? Who wouldn't come back?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the multicoloureds and Mr. Stevan Todorovic and some of his police officers, who sometimes did the same things that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you call anybody on the telephone afterwards?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I immediately went to the command, and from the command of the 4th Detachment, I called Captain Petrovic, in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did you talk about with the Captain, with Captain Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told Captain Petrovic that the people had left, that there were no problems during departure, that Mr. Makso was with them, and that I expected them to arrive there very quickly. And then I told him: Petrovic, I really didn't know what state these people were in. I don't know whether all of them were reach you alive. But I saw Grga Zubak, amongst others. I also saw a man called Gibic or Delic, who was also in a very sorry state. Could you please make sure that as soon as they get there, they receive medical assistance, because they seem to me to be in a terrible state. Mr. Petrovic told me that he would do everything, and I asked him, I told him that I would be at the command and when the people reached Brcko, I asked him to tell me that they had arrived, to let me know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did Mr. Petrovic call you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrovic called me. It was almost 12.00. They were supposed to travel for quite a while, because from Bosanski Samac to the JNA barracks in Brcko, it's over 45 to 50 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one more fact that needs to be established. What was the post of Mr. Petrovic at that time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic was the intelligence and security officer at the JNA barracks in Brcko, so he was the security officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The next day, or one of the following days, did you go to the Brcko barracks, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The very next day I left for Brcko. And I would like to say that when I arrived at the command, I told Commander Antic and deputy -- Captain Savic, how this action was carried out. And they knew that I was working for several days already to do everything to remove those people from Samac. And the next day, during the morning, I told Commander Antic that I wished to go to Brcko to see how these people are, and I personally wanted to show those people who had left, at least a little bit, that I was concerned about them and worried about all the things that they had been exposed to in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How did you get to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Brcko with Toso Tutnjevic, my driver. He was my permanent driver. He drove me and others. But he mostly drove me about, because I was the most active member of the command in the operative sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And who did you go to see in Brcko? Who did you meet in the Brcko barracks?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to Brcko, I first went to see Captain Petrovic, the colleague, and another man who was working in the security, Jovo Arsenic was working together with my colleague Petrovic in the intelligence and security organ of the barracks in Brcko. I wish to say that before I left for Brcko, Mr. Fadil Topcagic was also in front of the command, and he expressed a wish to go to Brcko and asked if there would be any obstacles to his going, because many of his closest friends and family were detained in the Territorial Defence, or had been detained in the Territorial Defence. And I said that as far as I was concerned, there was no obstacle. He then asked me if Lazar Stanisic, also known as Ziga, could also go with me [as interpreted], and whether they could buy some food, some cigarettes, and so on, and take this to those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Zaric will clarify this through his next answers, but here it says: "He then asked me," on page 53, line 24, "if Lazar Stanisic, also known as Ziga, could also go with me." Actually, it should read "with him," because he also went with Fadil Topcagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for the correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said to Mr. Topcagic that there was no problem, that they could go, because I knew how Mr. Lazar Stanisic, up to that moment, had behaved towards those people and what his opinion was. So I said there was no obstacle to their going. And they went in a white van to buy food in the town, and Toso Tutnjevic, my driver, and I went to the JNA barracks in Brcko directly. On arrival, I first went to see Captain Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, on that occasion, did you see, with Captain Petrovic, what the conditions were for those people?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as I arrived, Captain Petrovic told me that the people had been accommodated. He said: Grga is still alive. He was immediately given medical assistance. He and all the other detainees. He said the three of us will go now, meaning Jovo Arsenic, the man I mentioned, will go there to the place where those people are accommodated, to see them. The three of us, a few minutes later, went to the room where the people from Samac were accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, can you describe the facility and the rooms where the detainees from Samac were accommodated?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can. This was a room which, in my opinion, or according to my first impression, had been used as a warehouse for some sort of equipment, because there were two or three windows - I can't remember exactly how many - with bars that were inside the room. The bars were not on the outside wall, but they were inside, on the inside wall. And the rooms were quite large, airy, in comparison with what I had seen in Samac. The people were sitting on mattresses, as we called them. They were actually mats which had been given them to use. Some were sitting on them, some were lying down. And in these two rooms, they were in much better circumstances than what I had seen in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Had they been able to wash and shave?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had all washed, and quite a number of them had shaved. And those who hadn't shaved maybe hadn't had time to do so, or maybe they wanted to grow beards. But they looked much fresher at that moment, because they had been allowed, or at least that's what Petrovic told me, to go out, to wash, to use water. They could use the toilet normally. And when I arrived, there were two military policemen outside. Those were policemen with white belts, standing outside the building. They were under the control of the military police of the JNA barracks in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: On that day, did you see Mr. Fadil Topcagic and Lazar Stanisic in the Brcko barracks?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, but I heard that they had gone there. And when I was talking to Petrovic afterwards, I heard that they had arrived and brought something and that a colleague had gone so that they could hand over that food. But I wasn't with them at the moment when they were handing over the cigarettes and sandwiches, gear and other things they had brought for the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, on that day, was Mr. Milan Simic in your presence at any moment in that barracks?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Simic? No. Milan Simic wasn't there at all, not on that day, nor did I ever see him in the barracks in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Milan Simic ever go to the barracks in Brcko with you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I understand correctly, we are to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, and continue at 12.50 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, before the break we were saying that you were in the JNA barracks in Brcko with Mr. -- or rather, with Captain Petrovic. While you were with Captain Petrovic in Brcko, did anything else happen?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to say that when Captain Petrovic, Mr. Jovo Arsenic, and I entered the rooms I have described for the first time, I shook hands with all the detainees who were there and greeted them. There were two large rooms where they were accommodated, and a third smaller room, where there were Mr. Tihic, Mr. Lukac, and Grga Zubak. This was a smaller room, smaller than the other two big ones, but not really small, and there was a special military mattress there on which Mr. Grga was lying. In my conversation with them, I said, jokingly: Oh, there are quite a few of you here. And that was the first time that Safet Hadzialijagic said: There are over 50 of us here from Samac. And that was the first time that I learned how many people had arrived by truck that night, 56 people, who arrived from Bosanski Samac to the JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Only one small correction. On page 57, line 5, the number is 56. This is what Mr. Zaric said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The latter time it was 56, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then people spontaneously began to talk, and I stayed there for more than half an hour. Mr. Petrovic and Mr. Jovo Arsenic were with me. I remember, for example, Dr. Anto, the veterinarian I have mentioned, said to me: Simo, why did you push me among the politicians last night? You know that I'm in the HDZ, and Tudjman is in my heart. And this caused laughter among the detainees, because it might have been unimaginable for him to say that in some other circumstances. But what I'm trying to say is that the atmosphere was very relaxed when the vet, Dr. Anto, said that. In the corridor, I stopped briefly with Mr. Osman Jasarevic, also known as Roma, and I said: Well, how are things? And he said: The way they have to be. And I said: What will I say to the aunt? I was referring to his aunt, his mother's sister, who had worked with me for a long time in the same company, so we knew each other. And he said: Just say hello to her. And that was the brief chat I had with Mr. Osman Jasarevic. And when we entered the room where Mr. Dragan Lukac, Mr. Tihic, and the Grga Zubak were, where they were together in that room, then Mr. Petrovic said, jokingly, to Mr. Tihic: Tihic, tell me honestly, did you have anything to do with those barricades in Samac? And before Mr. Tihic replied, I said: He's got nothing to do with those barricades. Mr. Petrovic replied to that: If Zaric believes you, then very well. That's what we said, quite spontaneously.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What he said, does it mean let it be, like that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He used a word that is rarely used, and it's used only in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's a word used mostly by the Muslim population. And to add something else: Mr. Lukac then asked Petrovic whether there were any problems, because the three of them were not in those two big rooms where all the other detainees were. So he asked whether there were any obstacles for them to join the others, because they would feel more comfortable that way. They would be able to talk to people. And right away, Captain Petrovic said: There was no obstacle to that. And he said to the policemen: When we leave, let those men immediately go and join the others in the other two rooms. And later on I heard that that's what happened and that Mr. Tihic, Mr. Lukac, and Mr. Grga Zubak joined the other detainees in those other two rooms. And one thing more. At that moment, Grga Zubak had his eyes half open, so his condition was slightly better. He was able to talk to me briefly, and he said just: Simo, you know I'm not to blame for anything. And I said: Grga, don't worry. Just be patient a little bit. Get better. And that's all I talked about with Mr. Petrovic and those three colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And let me add just something else. In a conversation with Mr. Omer Nalic, who was also there, we chatted a bit, because we had been quite good friends before the war. We often spent time together. And I said: Omer, if I stay here a bit longer, we'll have a cup of coffee together. That was my message to him. Then Mr. Petrovic, Jovo Arsenic, and I went back to the office where they were working in the Brcko barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And tell us: Did you have coffee that day with Mr. Nalic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said since I'm not rushing that much, it would be good if Omer came and if we had coffee together. And then Jovo Arsenic went right away, as well as one of the military policemen, and Mr. Omer came later and he sat with us for about 45 to 50 minutes, for sure. And we were having coffee and we were all talking together: Myself, Mr. Arsenic, and Mr. Momcilo Petrovic, this Captain, as well as Mr. Nalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And on that occasion, Mr. Zaric, did you take any statement from Mr. Nalic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my intention, to tell you the truth. But when we began our conversation and we touched upon certain topics relating to the illegal arming of the SDA in Samac, and also about the involvement of certain persons in that, then Jovo Arsenic said then: This is the best opportunity for Omer to give a statement so that there would be no need to discuss this with him at a later date. And Omer at that point said that there wouldn't be any problem to do that. Whatever was necessary, he was at our disposal. And in the spontaneous conversation, notes were made of the talks that we had with him. He signed it on one side, and then on the other side I initialed it, indicating that this interview with him was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And when you were talking with Mr. Nalic, was any force or threat used against him?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No threats. We were having quite a pleasant conversation, that is, my experience of it, because we were drinking coffee, he was smoking cigarettes and talking with us in a normal way. There were no problems at all. And I said finally: Omer, would there be a problem for us now to take your statement and for you to sign it? He said no, there would be no problems. He would stand by that, and he signed it, and that is how it was. I'm not able to delve into how he personally felt but it was my feeling that he signed that without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak up.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The statement was given to Mr. Nalic. He read it alone by himself. He read it right through. He said there were no problems. Then he signed it, and after he signed it, I said: If you can put your signature down here, I can do that as well, and that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, you are too far from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you were compiling this statement, did you write down only what Mr. Nalic told you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only what Mr. Nalic told us, in a spontaneous conversation in front of everybody. Nothing was added or there was nothing else in that statement other than what he himself told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, did you conduct any interviews with Mr. Hasan Bicic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day I had two more interviews only. One of them was with Hasan Bicic and the other interview was with his brother, Muhamed Bicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Mr. Zaric be shown Exhibit D8/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: While the exhibit is being found, Mr. Zaric: Were you aware of the activities of Mr. Hasan Bicic on the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I already had information about how he was one of the people amongst the members of the armed formations of the SDA that were in town, that he was in several places, that he was armed, he as well as his brother and some other people. So I had this information because I saw this from the statements and the interviews that he had already had at the public security station in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the statement. This is Mr. Hasan Bicic's statement.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the statement of Mr. Muhamed, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I said D8/4. D8/4 is the statement of Hasan Bicic, while D9/4 is the statement of Muhamed Bicic. Look at the document, please, just to familiarise yourself. You can take it from the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now I remember this quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, is this the statement you took from Mr. Hasan Bicic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In that statement, did you write down what Mr. Hasan Bicic told you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only what he told me. And I must say that the atmosphere during the conversation with Mr. Bicic was very pleasant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were any threats used, or force against him?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, as you mentioned a little while ago, you said that you knew about certain activities of Hasan Bicic during the 17th of April, before you took this statement.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't put down this information that you had in the statement?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put down only what Mr. Hasan said to me. Mr. Jovo Arsenic was next to me, while Mr. Bicic was giving us this statement. So I put down just what he told me. I didn't really ask any questions, nor did I broaden the scope of our interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did Mr. Bicic sign this statement without any threats or coercion?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did that without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't need the document any longer. You already said that you also had an interview with Mr. Muhamed Bicic.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is Mr. Hasan's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Mr. Zaric be given Exhibit D9/4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, while that's being done, could I again ask that my friend Mr. Pisarevic not lead on these sorts of issues? There's a few questions which he's led. There are ways of asking what are the circumstances of the taking of the statement, did he sign it, what happened? He's put words in the witness's mouth a few times. That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I am sure Mr. Pisarevic will remember not to do that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. I'm trying, but it's possible that some questions like that were put, but I will really try to avoid that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, will you please familiarise yourself with the statement.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this statement quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Is that the statement that you compiled during the interview with Mr. Bicic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the statement, based on the interview that I conducted. Mr. Jovo Arsenic was present with me also. And after the statement was completed, I signed it, and the same statement was signed also by Mr. Muhamed Bicic, without any problems. He familiarised himself with the statement, in detail, and he didn't have any remarks about the text. And I would like to say that the statement was given in normal circumstances, without any coercion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were you familiar with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just a moment. Who printed this document out? Did you, Mr. Zaric, do it, or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This document was typed by Mr. Jovo Arsenic, who was one of the staff members there at the premises of the JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: But it takes some time to print out such a document. What did you do while it was printed out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While the document was being printed, I dictated the statement which Mr. Bicic was listening to, and Mr. Arsenic was typing it. So Mr. Bicic would say something, I would dictate the sentence, and then Mr. Arsenic would type it out. And the same procedure was used for Mr. Hasan, as well as for Mr. Nalic. I would say a sentence out loud and the other person was listening, and then typing out what I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that Mr. Muhamed Bicic was doing any actions on the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This information I was familiar with, but this was not put into the statement. The statement contains only what Muhamed Bicic said during the interview at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you know that Muhamed Bicic was doing on the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My information was such that he was one of the members of the militarily organised unit of Muslims in town, that he was seen at several places in the centre of town, near the mosque, near the department store, in the Djure Djakovica Street, so that this information was -- and of course, he was armed, and then he came back with those weapons and many neighbours saw him. But this piece of information was not exploited, nor did we mention anything about this during our interview in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was any coercion used in the case of Mr. Muhamed Bicic, any threats or any force?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No threats and no force was used. I was dictating the statement out loud, and besides that, he also read the statement in full afterwards and then put his signature on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you actually put into the statement?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Authentically what Mr. Muhamed Bicic stated during the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, over the next few days, were you interested in the circumstances and the conditions in which the detainees from Samac were kept at the Brcko barracks?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would call Mr. Petrovic every day. Sometimes I would speak to him, sometimes I would speak with Mr. Jovo Arsenic. This person that I mentioned before. And besides this, on the 27th and on the 28th, Mr. Topcagic went to Brcko privately with his van, and he took them a lot of underwear and a lot of other things, so I was able to hear from him about the conditions for the prisoners. But every day I would ask about their circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have an opportunity to see again any of the people who were detained at the Brcko barracks?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: On which occasion was this?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was on the 29th of April, 1992, in the premises of the public security station, when a TV crew from Television Novi Sad taped an interview with some members, amongst whom were several people who had been in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember and tell Their Honours who these people were who were brought from Brcko to give an interview to Television Novi Sad in the police station in Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the people brought from Brcko were Mr. Sulejman Tihic, Omer Nalic, Safet Hadzialijagic, also known as Coner. I think that those three arrived in Samac from Brcko and gave an interview to Novi Sad Television.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, we'll now discuss that interview a little. Did you participate, or rather, did you give an interview to Novi Sad Television?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How did it come about that it was you, of all people, who gave an interview to Television Novi Sad on the 29th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in the morning of the 29th of April, 1992, the duty officer said he had Commander Nikolic on the line and that he wanted to speak to me. I spoke to the commander over the communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did you talk about with Mr. Nikolic, the commander of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Nikolic said to me that on that day a television crew from Novi Sad Television would be arriving in Samac, that they had been in the command of the 17th Tactical Group the day before, and that he had given them an interview, and he told me to prepare. And when talking to these people, to say something about the documentation connected to the war plan of the Party of Democratic Action and the HDZ, in connection with their preparations for an attack or for an armed struggle on the territory of Bosanski Samac. I was to do this because, after seeing the material and the official notes, which I had become familiar with, I took it to the command of the 17th Tactical Group, several days later, as far as I know, so that Commander Nikolic knew that I had the information about this plan and these activities undertaken by the paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How did you understand this conversation of yours with Commander Nikolic about your participation in the interview?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he knew I didn't have much time but that I should stick to the documents quite strictly and express my opinion about them. I saw this as an order from my commander to contribute to this conversation, so that as soon as I received this task, I looked at the documents again in order to refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And where was this interview taped?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interview was taped in the public security station, on the second floor, in the office used by the chief of the public security station, Mr. Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And who called you to come to the police station to give an interview?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was called by the duty officer from the public security station, who said that the television crew from Novi Sad had arrived and that they were expecting me to turn up, and he had been told this by the police commander. The police commander had told him to contact me. The police commander at the time was Mr. Savo Cancarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And when you arrived in the police station, where did you go and who did you meet?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the police station, and upstairs, I went to the office I had been told to go to, and in Mr. Todorovic's office, I found a journalist, who I think introduced himself as Minja. There was also a cameraman who was there with his equipment. And in Mr. Todorovic's office, there was, besides Stevan Todorovic, also Dragan Todorovic, also known as Crni [as interpreted]. That's the situation I found when I entered that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And how did this interview proceed? Who put questions to you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I was introduced to Mr. Minja, he said he had been to see my commander, that the commander had told him about me, and I said that I had come. And he said he wanted to talk to me about the materials we had at our disposal in connection with the war plans of the Party of Democratic Action and the HDZ, in connection with preparations for an armed struggle in the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: After this conversation, did he tell you what you were to do then?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said: All right. No problem. I've brought the documents with me. When you're ready, here I am. And he said: Can we start right away? And I said: Yes, of course. There was a large conference table there, and the journalist was sitting on one side and I was sitting at the table on the other side, with the documentation in front of me. The cameraman was filming all this from a corner, and in quite another part of the office, Mr. Todorovic and Crni were sitting on two chairs, and they were only observing me while I was putting forward this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. Just on the matter of the person otherwise known as Crni: We need to have a correction in the transcript, on page 68, line 13, because it says, "Dragan Todorovic, also known as Crni." So we don't want anyone to get confused there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, in that room where the interview was conducted, apart from you, the journalist from TV Novi Sad, and the cameraman from TV Novi Sad, while you were being interviewed, who else was present in that room?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stevan Todorovic, as the chief of the public security station, and Dragan Djordjevic, also known as Crni, one of the leaders of the Specials who had arrived in Bosanski Samac from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, will you please describe the course of the interview between you and the journalist from TV Novi Sad. Did he put questions to you? Did you answer? Did you show the documents? Tell us what this looked like.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was typical kind of interview. He was putting questions, I was answering. Sometimes my replies were brief, sometimes they were lengthier, depending on my use of a certain document in order to clarify some of my opinions and standpoints in connection with the war plans and the role of these armed paramilitary formations on the territory of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How long did this interview last, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My interview was maybe half an hour long, at the most, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you remember who was interviewed after you by the journalist from TV Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the exact order, but I know that after me, Mr. Tihic, Mr. Omer Nalic, Mr. Safet Hadzialijagic, also known as Coner, Mr. Izet Izetbegovic, also known as Izo; and Mr. Nizam Ramusovic, aka Tota, one of the members of the 4th Detachment who was wounded in that incident that we have mentioned quite a few times here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And how was the interview conducted with the other participants you have just enumerated, for example, with Mr. Sulejman Tihic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just say: When I completed my part of the interview, I went into the next two rooms, and I could see Mr. Vlado Sarkanovic, who told me that Tihic and some other people from Brcko were in the next room, and he said Tihic asked you to stick around. He doesn't want you to leave. He's afraid. And I said: No problem. I'll stay in the police station for as long as the TV crew is here, bearing in mind this request. Although had somebody wanted to do something, I don't know whether I would have been in a situation to oppose it, but he felt safer with me around. So that's why I remained on the premises of the public security station, and I was there for a while, while Mr. Tihic was being interviewed by the journalist from Novi Sad Television.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you go to the police station in Bosanski Samac to give that interview? I mean when you did, did you know that there would be other people interviewed?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know who would be interviewed or who would be there. I was the first one to be interviewed, and then I heard that Tihic and the others were there, but I had no idea who would be interviewed on that day, who else would be interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it now time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn now. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, were you present during the interview by the TV Novi Sad journalist with Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who else was in the room?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic was present the entire time, and at one point, Mr. Crni came to the door. He said something to Mr. Tihic and then went back out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, can you tell us why you were there? Why were you present?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry. Excuse me. Just before you move on, I was just waiting to see whether you were going to ask Mr. Zaric: What did Crni say to Mr. Tihic? Mr. Zaric, you just said that he came to the door, he said something to Mr. Tihic, and then went back out. Do you recall or do you know what he said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember. The camera had to stop rolling because he wasn't really paying too much attention to that, the camera had to stop, and he told Mr. Tihic: When this is over, we need to see each other so that I can see what these spies of yours are reporting, so that we are being hit by these guys from Croatia. Something to the effect that Mr. Tihic should know that some of his people from Samac were passing on information so that Samac would be shelled. He said something that had the effect of confusing Mr. Tihic. It confused me, it confused [Realtime transcript read in error "accused"] the cameraman, as well as the reporter. But I assume that this was just a sort of scenario between Mr. Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, and Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: A small correction in the transcript. On page 72, line 14, it confused the cameraman, not accused the cameraman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And just one other question on that, Mr. Zaric: When you say that you assumed that this was just a sort of scenario between Crni and Mr. Stevan Todorovic, what do you mean by that exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I mean is I remember one detail when I commented on some of my own stands, when I was expressing them to the reporter at one point when I was giving my own assessment about the situation in Samac. At one point while Mr. Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, and Stevan Todorovic were in the room, Todorovic, the chief of the public security station, they said: Take care also to commend our men also. Of course, I didn't show at that point any fear in front of the camera, but later I had that remark of his in mind. I'm not trying to justify any of the assessments I made then in that interview, but I felt that they wanted that interview that was being conducted to be in accordance with some kind of scenario that they wanted us to pay attention to the Serb national structure, and also to speak in favour of the Serbian point of view. And this is what I meant when I said the screenplay, the scenario. This is what I wanted to back up by an example of my own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And after this appearance by Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, did the interview continue?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The interview with Mr. Tihic was resumed, and I can just say that the representative of Novi Sad Television asked Mr. Tihic and the other participants in the interview, and I would say that he did this in a professional way: Do you wish to give this interview freely, and what you are saying, are you stating of this of your own free will? And all of them, more or less, responded affirmatively to those questions, that they were providing the interview of their own free will and that there were no problems. But I can assume, and that is my opinion, how they felt as people who were brought from prison, brought in front of the camera, and how they felt when they had to say that everything was all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you please tell us: Why did you stay in that room?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only reason why I stayed was because of Mr. Tihic's request, so that there would be no problems, just in case there were problems. I believe that my presence would, to a certain extent, prevent any excesses from taking place, because they were in Samac before they had suffered much, and now they were in the area of Brcko, and that was the only reason why I found myself in that situation and remained in the room while the interviews were being conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were you present during the interviews given by Mr. Nalic, Mr. Hadzialijagic, Mr. Izet Izetbegovic, Mr. Ramusovic, Nizam?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire time while these people were giving their interviews, I was in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The people who gave these interviews, did they go back to Brcko; and if so, how did they do that? Could you please tell us what you did so that they would safely go back to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the interview with the reporter were completed, they were in one room, and they came from Brcko with a military vehicle, escorted by several military policemen. And in conversation with Vlado Sarkanovic, who was there, and with Milos Savic, Mr. Fadil Topcagic was also there later, we only said that it would be good for them to go back as soon as possible. And Mr. Tihic himself, as well as Mr. Nalic and Mr. Hadzialijagic, sensed this atmosphere, and they said that it would be the best thing for them to leave the premises of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did they go back to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very quickly after that they sat in -- they entered this police vehicle, this Land Rover [as interpreted], and they went to Brcko. Afterwards, I spoke with Mr. Petrovic and received the information that they came back safely and that there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, when you mentioned this Land Rover now, the transcript said that this was a police vehicle. Was this a police vehicle or a military vehicle?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was a military vehicle. It was a Pinzgauer vehicle. It's a smaller vehicle that can fit seven to eight soldiers or police officers inside. And when I say police officers, I mean military police officers. This is a military vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, in this interview, you already mentioned that you used certain documents about the military organising and the illegal arming of the Party for Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would now ask for the witness to be shown Exhibit D14/4. This is a list of self-organised citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, could you please look at this document.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Is this one of the documents that you used while conducting the interview?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was one of the documents I used in the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown document D25/4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Mr. Counsel, which document are you now referring to? The one brought ahead of Mr. Zaric or the one you are now bringing in front of him?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the document about the military organising of a unit of Muslims from Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think there's a confusion, because it says D14/4 on line 16, and then on line 24 it says D25/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it would be clearer if the witness could be given document D25/4. The document -- the second document is marked D25/4, and that is this first document, where it says "the engineering sabotage platoon." The first -- the document was separated. The first three pages were marked as document D26/4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are talking about document D25/4, and this is the second time that same thing happens. This document was tendered into evidence, but not in its entirety. First three pages were marked for ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And the rest were fully admitted into evidence. So this is document D25/4, with first three pages which are marked only for identification. And that is the first document that we are discussing now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, could you please look at this document.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Is that one of the documents that you used during the interview?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Pardon. With whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interview that Mr. Zaric gave to the reporter of TV Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The document can stay in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown document D26/4 now. That is the document about mobilisation, the mobilisation of the unit, the military unit of members of the Muslim ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've looked at the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you use this document as well, Mr. Zaric, and did you show this document while you were giving the interview to the reporter of TV Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us now, Mr. Zaric, if you know: Who discovered these documents?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw these documents for the first time at the criminal investigations department. Mr. Milos Savic showed them to me, and Vlado Sarkanovic, who were working at the public security station at the time, and they told me that the complete documentation was found by Mr. Milan Jekic, who was carrying out the function of deputy commander of the public security station, and that he found the documents in one of the rooms in the lower part of the public security station which he was using for his own needs at the time the commander of the reserve police forces of Samac, Mr. Namik Suljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You used all three of these documents when you were giving the interview to TV Novi Sad; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I used all of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When did Milos Savic and Mr. Vlado Sarkanovic show you these documents for the first time at the public security station at the criminal investigations department, were these documents all bound together as one set?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were bound together as one set.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if anybody added anything to these documents or did anything or worked on these documents in any way?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could see initially, some names were added to these documents, such as Pop, Coner, and so on. But as far as I remember, all these documents, all these war plans, were -- they were not bound in a cover or anything, but they were on the table of the chief of the crime investigations department, on his desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the first three pages of those documents?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: That is, D25/4, did you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't need these documents any more, but I would like to note that in view of the fact that in the course of investigative -- in the course of these proceedings, witnesses who have testified before the Trial Chamber before also discussed these documents, and they are Stevan Todorovic, on the 19th of June, 2002; on the 13th of March, Witness Vlado Sarkanovic discussed the document; and that this topic was covered by Witness Milan Jekic, under testimonies under Rule 71, in Belgrade; and that today, Mr. Zaric testified about these documents. I would repeat the request of the Defence, that the first three pages of document D25/4 have the marking ID removed and that they be admitted into the evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What is the position of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. The position of the Prosecution is the same as it's been throughout the case. The person who drafted this document testified last year about this whole pile of documents. He admitted to what he did, his plan, the reason for drafting them, and he testified that the first three pages were falsified, and he testified about all the rest of these, which allowed most of these to be admitted. And when he indicated that they were falsified, he explained why they were falsified. Up to this point, the evidence has been the same. These documents were seized from one of three different places, that they wound up in the police station, and at some time later, that they're found. There is no change in the evidence today as it was a year ago, other than Alija Fitozovic's testimony, which he says: I put these documents together. The first three pages of this document have been falsified. Other than that, I've put everything else together. And because of that, the testimony as to falsification of the documents, they have been -- the first three pages have been left as an ID. There is nothing new today, there is nothing new in Milan Jekic's statement in Belgrade, there was nothing new in Todorovic's statement. Todorovic didn't know if he had seen the document from anywhere from two to four to five days, could even have been a week after they had been seized. So we're back at the same situation that we were a year ago, and repetition doesn't make them admissible. Repetition of the same information. We're still at the information from the person who drafted it, who said: I've drafted all of it, but the first three pages, those were falsified. And unless they can come up with some information to establish authenticity, other than people who -- through hearsay learned that they somehow were found, that they were seized, and that they had seen them several days after being found, or several days later, we're still at the same position as we were a year ago. So we would oppose this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If I may reply to my colleague, very briefly. We do believe that there is a very significant development in this case regarding these first three pages of document D25/4. First of all, it is undisputed that in the statement of Mr. Milan Jekic, which was taken in Belgrade under Rule 71, it is in his statement that he was the one who actually found these documents and about the place where these documents have been found. So from -- as the person who actually found the documents, we have a chain of custody of these documents from that very moment. Secondly, Mr. Alija Fitozovic didn't say, if I can remember correctly, that he himself faked these three pages. He said that he drafted the document but that some parts of these pages are not the one that he drafted and that he assumes that they are faked. After that, we have testimony of Mr. Sarkanovic, who identified these documents and the ones that were used by him and other investigators in the SUP who actually presented these documents, and finally, we have now statement of Mr. Zaric, who also recognised these documents as the one that he received from Mr. Savic and Mr. Sarkanovic in the SUP. So we do have a chain of custody from the person who actually found these documents in SUP, up until this moment, when they were tendered into evidence of this Tribunal. And I would like to have the same standards of this Tribunal as for the document that we are referring as documents A and B. Let them be introduced into evidence, these first three pages, and the Trial Chamber will of course decide what weight would it give to these first three pages of the document. Because obviously, Alija Fitozovic has a very good reason to say the first three pages were faked, and we are all -- the Defence is all aware of what reason could it be. I don't want to argue this. I will save our arguments for our final brief, why Mr. Fitozovic said a thing like that. But if the Trial Chamber decides other way, we would like to reserve our right for some additional graphological expertise of these three pages, and that possibly could be -- we thought this would be enough, giving a full chain of custody for these documents, we thought that would be enough for admittance of these documents into evidence. But if not, then we have to find some other way to introduce them into evidence with some expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I respond to one thing very briefly, less than 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There is no full chain of custody. The person who found it did not know how those documents got there, did not know who drafted those documents, did not know who typed them. It's a partial chain of custody. It's from the time that they get there on. So we're still without authenticity. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But Mr. Weiner, is it not significant that the larger part of the document of this group of documents were accepted by Alija Fitozovic and it's only three first three that have been disputed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And I think it is significant, because you have the person who was the author of them who said that he was the one who drafted them and put them together, and he allowed this stuff to come in by saying this stuff is mine. This stuff are just forgeries, these three pages. And it's almost a declaration against interest. He's admitting that he put all this stuff together. He admitted that he put together the plans of where the different power plants and power stations were in case they decided during wartime to bomb them. He made some major admissions. But he's saying, I did that stuff, I did that stuff, but this stuff is not mine. And I think that's very strong evidence that this is not from his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I add something to this? I don't want to repeat anything that was already said, but this concerns all the Defence teams. Mr. Fitozovic did admit to some documents that put him in a direct connection with the TO and the police and the SDA offices at the time, and that's the letter to the republican TO. But what I think is of fundamental importance here, I wish to add to what Mr. Lazarevic said. It is just a question of whom the Chamber will decide to believe. We know how this document was found and how, in the police station, this document could have a link with Mr. Fitozovic. But whether the Chamber will believe Mr. Fitozovic or Mr. Zaric, it's up to the Trial Chamber. But we have demonstrated a very strong, direct line. That is why I think that we have indicated through our evidence a clear line as to how these documents reached the Trial Chamber and whether the Chamber will believe Fitozovic or Zaric and the other witnesses who claim the opposite, only the Chamber can decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And Your Honour, if I may just have a few words on behalf of defence of Dr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I fully -- I'm in full accordance with the previous words of my learned friends. Unless it is not disputed fact for the Prosecution that the SDA and HDZ in Samac were arming themselves and preparing for takeover and all other facts, then we could maybe discuss on the other positions. If it's not the case on the side of Prosecution, in accordance with previous practice, I just would like to respectfully remind this Trial Chamber, we've got a lengthy and detailed discussions and submissions with regard to the so-called -- document so-called variant A and B, and as far as my recollection serves me, I think that this Honourable Trial Chamber took the position that by the end of the trial, during the process of rendering of judgement, the weight will be -- the weight of that evidence will be discussed. So I think the same should apply for this particular case. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber will admit them. It's a matter of weight. And also, it will depend on how the evidence will be analysed, as documents indicating whatever the evidence will indicate or authored by whoever the evidence will indicate. So they will be admitted into evidence for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have a number, or shall we keep the same number, D25/4, instead of an ID number, for the first three pages?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It will be D25/4. It will be a complete document, that's all. So it will retain the same number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you mentioned that on that day, the 29th of April, Novi Sad Television also interviewed Mr. Izet Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know from where Izet Izetbegovic was brought to give that interview?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I only saw him in the office in front of the office of the chief of the public security station. But where he was accommodated and where he was brought from, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know where he was taken after he gave the interview?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you present, Mr. Zaric, in the police station when Mr. Izet Izetbegovic talked over the telephone with Alija Izetbegovic [as interpreted], the then president of the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the police station?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw Mr. Izet Izetbegovic in the public security station on one occasion only, and that was when he was interviewed. I did not have other opportunities to see him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what happened later to Izet Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later I did learn certain things that Mr. Izetbegovic was taken to Belgrade by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear later that he had been exchanged?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but all this was information that reached me later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Zaric, we will now move on to a different topic. Mr. Zaric, when you were appointed head for national security of the Bosanski Samac municipality -- before we go on to discuss this, could Mr. Zaric be shown Exhibit P81.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise to the Chamber, but I need to say something more about these detainees, if the Chamber will allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zaric, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wish to say that on the 1st of May, 1992, I received a telephone call from Mr. Petrovic, the captain who was performing the duty of the OB organ in the Brcko barracks of the JNA. He told me that war had broken out in Brcko and that the bridge over the River Gunja, or rather, over the River Sava, had been destroyed during the night. And this was the bridge between Brcko and a place called Gunja, which is on the opposite bank, that is, in the Republic of Croatia. He said that the situation in Brcko was almost out of control and that he had talked to Makso Simeunovic and Commander Nikolic, telling them that these people who had been brought in from Samac and who were in the JNA barracks could no longer be safe there. Then I said to Mr. Petrovic: What can be done with these people without bringing them back to this hell in Samac? Because in Samac, people are being killed every day. The situation is out of control and I don't know what can happen to them if they're brought back. Mr. Petrovic told me he had already made certain efforts in agreement with Commander Nikolic and Makso, and that he had called a barracks commander in Bijeljina and asked him to have these people taken to the barracks in Bijeljina, the JNA barracks which were then not affected by war, because there were no war operations going on in Bijeljina at the time. I said: Do whatever you can, but don't send them to Samac, to this hell. And in the afternoon, Mr. Petrovic informed me that he had succeeded in having all the detainees from Samac transferred to the barracks in Brcko [as interpreted] and that they were safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Zaric. Now that you have broached this topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm wondering about -- yes, line 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Page 86, line -- it's here line -- barracks in Bijeljina, actually. They were transferred to Bijeljina. It was not in dispute. Not in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether these detainees who were taken from Brcko to Bijeljina were ever returned to Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Afterwards I received information, in mid-May, that a certain number of detainees from Bijeljina had been brought back to Bosanski Samac and accommodated in the primary school in Bosanski Samac or, more precisely, in the gym of the primary school in Bosanski Samac, and the detainees who had arrived -- it was from then that we learned that some of the people who had been with them had been transferred by helicopter to another place, and we later on learned that they had been taken to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn afterwards who were the people who were transferred and where they were transferred to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We learned later on that among those who had gone to Batajnica was Mr. Tihic, Mr. Lukac, Sejo Mujkanovic, one of the policemen, Dr. Miroslav --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You mean Kedacic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Kedacic. Then there was Franjo Barukcic. These are the names I remember, but I can't remember all of them. And I know that afterwards Mr. Izo Izetbegovic also went. You've already asked me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You've already said that. Have you looked at this document, P81, which is a decision on your appointment as chief for national security of the municipality of Samac? Is this the document?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When were you first told about this, and when was this document handed to you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it was on the same day. Whether it was on the 29th or the 30th, when I received a phone call from the Crisis Staff. It was Mitar Mitrovic, the secretary of the Crisis Staff, and he said I should come to the Crisis Staff because I was needed there. I went to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And when you arrived, did you report to the secretary of the Crisis Staff, Mitar Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And then he told me that the Crisis Staff had reached a decision and issued a document appointing me chief of the national security service in a state of emergency. I looked at the document and asked Mr. Blagoje Simic, the president of the Crisis Staff, to receive me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, before this decision was adopted, did anybody consult you or ask you if you wanted to accept such a post, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody asked me anything. I was called to come, and then this decision was just handed to me, like I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was it possible for you to meet Mr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had that conversation, myself and Mr. Simic, that very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did you tell Mr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked Blagoje: What happened? How did it come about that I am appointed chief for national security, without anybody discussing that with me first? Mr. Blagoje Simic told me that there was an initiative at one of the most recent meetings of the Crisis Staff about the need to appoint a chief for national security, and that at the proposal of some people, my name was put forward, and that he personally, as the president of the Crisis Staff, didn't have anything against that, and that is why this decision was issued. He said that he was led by my previous experience, by the fact that I worked in the state security service before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that at the municipal level, someone is appointed chief for national security? Could you please explain this procedure, the structure of this service, a little bit. This national security, is that the former state security? How do you understand that term?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the actual topic that I discussed with Mr. Blagoje. I told him first that I don't understand, that this is a completely new title for me, national security service, and I asked him if that had anything to do with the state security service and the method of work of the service where I worked until 1991. Then this decision is illegal. The municipal body, any municipal body, cannot appoint me as chief of national security because this was directly in the hierarchy of the state security sector, which, in the organisational sense, is part of the ministry of the internal affairs of Republika Srpska.
